verdict.rationale: One body of vocabulary places the Son before creation and inside the divine being. John 1:1 uses the imperfect of being (eimi, morph V-IAI-3S) three times for ho logos at the arche, contrasted with the aorist ginomai of created things, John 17:5 and 17:24 set shared glory and the Father's love for me pro tou ton kosmon einai and pro katabolēs kosmou, Colossians 1:15-17 makes the Son the sphere, agent, and goal of all creation and pro pantōn, Hebrews 1:6 calls him ton prōtotokon already when God brings him into the world, and the sending verbs act on a Son already monogenēs (apostellō perfect in 1 John 4:9, didōmi aorist in John 3:16). But a second body of vocabulary, the begetting verbs yalad (Ps 2:7, Qal perfect) and gennaō (Heb 1:5, 5:5, Acts 13:33, perfect gegennēka with sēmeron, today), is attached by the canon to a moment in time, the resurrection and enthronement, and Hebrews 1:5b quotes the Davidic adoption formula of 2 Samuel 7:14. The begetting words alone do not rank these two patterns, so the affirm rests on the durative and pre-creation terms, not on the begetting terms.

scripture.force: ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, with ἦν tagged V-IAI-3S (imperfect of εἰμί) three times, placing the Logos in durative being at the absolute origin, with the πρὸς τὸν θεόν relation. Verse 3 shifts to the aorist ἐγένετο for created things, so the Logos stands on the uncreated side of the was, came-to-be contrast.
οὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεόν repeats the imperfect ἦν and the πρός relation, locking the Father and Logos distinction into the pre-creation frame before any begetting language appears.

δόξαν ὡς μονογενοῦς παρὰ πατρός pairs μονογενής with παρὰ πατρός. The same word μονογενής is used in the canon of ordinary only-children (Luke 7:12, Luke 8:42, Heb 11:17 of Isaac), so it lexically means only, unique-kind, not created or originated.

μονογενὴς θεός (earliest witnesses) or ὁ μονογενὴς υἱός (Byzantine), ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πατρός. The present participle ὁ ὤν marks ongoing relational location, not an event of becoming Son. Both variant readings apply μονογενής to the Son.

δόξασόν με σύ, πάτερ, παρὰ σεαυτῷ τῇ δόξῃ ᾗ εἶχον πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι παρὰ σοί. The imperfect εἶχον with πρό plus genitive places shared glory and the παρὰ σοί relation prior to the existence of the κόσμος.

ἠγάπησάς με πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, with aorist ἠγάπησάς and πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου locating the Father's love directed at me before the foundation of the world. The object of that love is the personal me of the speaker, prior to creation.

εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου, πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως. πρωτότοκος (9 occurrences) carries both birth-order firstborn (Luke 2:7) and rank or preeminence (read against v.16 ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα). The grounding ὅτι makes him agent of all creation, so the genitive is of rank, not membership in κτίσις.

ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα, then perfect τὰ πάντα δι' αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν ἔκτισται. The triad ἐν, διά, εἰς makes the Son the sphere, agent, and goal of all creation. If τὰ πάντα is created in and through him, he is not a member of τὰ πάντα.

καὶ αὐτός ἐστιν πρὸ πάντων, καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκεν. Emphatic αὐτός with present ἐστιν plus πρό marks personal priority over τὰ πάντα, and the perfect συνέστηκεν marks his ongoing sustaining function.

ὅταν δὲ πάλιν εἰσαγάγῃ τὸν πρωτότοκον εἰς τὴν οἰκουμένην. The Son is already named τὸν πρωτότοκον at the point God brings him into the inhabited world, so the firstborn status precedes his entry into the world rather than being conferred by it.

πρὸς δὲ τὸν υἱόν: ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ θεός, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος. The Father addresses the Son with the vocative ὁ θεός and an everlasting throne, citing Ps 45:6 (store cross-ref Heb.1.8 to Ps.45.6) as direct divine address to the Son.

ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ. ἀπαύγασμα (radiance) and χαρακτήρ (exact impress) describe origin-from but not temporal beginning. Radiance is co-temporal with its source, so the lexis describes derivation without a point of coming-to-be.

τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ τὸν μονογενῆ ἀπέσταλκεν ὁ θεὸς εἰς τὸν κόσμον. ἀπέσταλκεν is tagged V-RAI-3S (perfect), and the Son is already qualified μονογενῆ when sent. The sending acts on an existing unique Son, it does not make him Son.
τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ τὸν μονογενῆ ἔδωκεν. ἔδωκεν is tagged V-AAI-3S (aorist), acting on a Son already designated μονογενῆ. The giving does not constitute the sonship.

The Hebrew frames the line as a חֹק (choq, decree) the LORD spoke: בְּנִי אַתָּה, הַיּוֹם יְלִדְתִּיךָ. יְלִדְתִּיךָ is yalad tagged HVqp1cs (Qal perfect 1cs with 2ms suffix). yalad occurs 466 times and dominantly means literal physical begetting (Genesis genealogies), so its native sense is point-of-origin, but here it is the content of a decree spoken הַיּוֹם, today, a coronation idiom. The word carries origin sense but its frame is enthronement declaration.

υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε, with γεγέννηκά tagged V-RAI-1S (perfect) plus the adverb σήμερον (today). The verse then quotes 2 Sam 7:14 (store cross-ref Heb.1.5 to 2Sam.7.14) in the future, ἔσομαι αὐτῷ εἰς πατέρα καὶ αὐτὸς ἔσται μοι εἰς υἱόν, the Davidic covenant formula. The begetting plus today plus future adoption formula is a royal-installation matrix.

ἀναστήσας Ἰησοῦν ... υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε. The aorist participle ἀναστήσας (having raised up) ties the σήμερον of the begetting decree explicitly to the resurrection day, so the canon itself applies the begetting language of Ps 2:7 to a moment in time.

διὸ καὶ τὸ γεννώμενον ἅγιον κληθήσεται υἱὸς θεοῦ. The future passive κληθήσεται (will be called) and the present participle τὸ γεννώμενον (the one being born) attach the title Son of God to the one conceived and born, so the sonship title is here predicated of the incarnate child. The verb is called, which does not by itself decide whether the title names a pre-existing relation or originates at birth.

יהוה קָנָנִי רֵאשִׁית דַּרְכּוֹ. The verb qanah carries possess or acquire as well as create. LXX renders ἔκτισέν με, used against eternal sonship, but the subject is personified Wisdom in poetry, and identifying that figure with the Son is a typological judgment, not a direct lemma identification of the Son.

complicating_texts.resolution: הַיּוֹם יְלִדְתִּיךָ uses yalad (Qal perfect), whose dominant canon sense across 466 occurrences is literal physical begetting, a point of origin. Here it is the content of a חֹק (decree) spoken הַיּוֹם (today), the royal-coronation idiom of the Davidic Psalms. The begetting word supplies an origin sense, but the today frame redirects it to an enthronement declaration of an already addressed son, so the verse neither establishes nor excludes eternal sonship on lexis alone.

σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε (perfect with today) is paired in the same verse with the future Davidic adoption formula of 2 Sam 7:14, ἔσομαι ... εἰς πατέρα, ἔσται ... εἰς υἱόν. Acts 13:33 fixes the σήμερον to the resurrection. So the canon applies the begetting and son-installation language to a moment in time, which is why the begetting texts cannot by themselves carry the eternal verdict. The affirm rests on the separate durative and pre-creation vocabulary, not on these verses.

ἀναστήσας Ἰησοῦν fixes the σήμερον of Ps 2:7 to the resurrection day. This corroborates that the begetting decree is applied as public declaration at an event, not as a statement about the Son coming into existence. It complicates but does not overturn, since the Johannine and Pauline pre-creation terms describe a relation already in place.

κληθήσεται υἱὸς θεοῦ (future passive, will be called) attaches the title Son of God to τὸ γεννώμενον, the one being conceived and born. The verb called does not lexically decide whether the title names a pre-existing relation now revealed in the incarnation or originates at conception. The word underdetermines the question, so this remains unresolved at the lexical level and is the clearest single-verse pressure point against an eternal reading.

πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως in isolation can read as first member of κτίσις. The causal ὅτι in v.16 makes him the agent in whom and through whom τὰ πάντα was created, which rules out membership in τὰ πάντα. πρωτότοκος (9 occurrences) bears both birth-order and rank senses, and Heb 1:6 shows the Son is already πρωτότοκος before being brought into the world, so rank or preeminence is the contextually forced sense here.

Hebrew קָנָנִי is ambiguous between acquire and create, and LXX ἔκτισέν με was used in the fourth-century dispute. Lexically the identification of personified Wisdom with the pre-incarnate Son is a typological judgment, not a direct lemma identification, so this verse does not by itself overturn the Johannine and Pauline pattern.

ὁ πατὴρ μείζων μού ἐστιν has been read against co-equal sonship. μείζων in this discourse follows the sending and return frame (ὑπάγω πρὸς τὸν πατέρα), addressing ordering during the incarnation, not a temporal-beginning vocabulary for the Son.

variant_units_examined.note: Earliest witnesses (P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) read μονογενὴς θεός, the Byzantine tradition reads ὁ μονογενὴς υἱός. Both apply μονογενής to the Son in the bosom of the Father with the present participle ὁ ὤν, so the verdict holds across both readings.

The variant at the end of the verse reads ῥάβδος τῆς βασιλείας αὐτοῦ versus σου. Either reading preserves the address ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ θεός to the Son, so the everlasting kingdom predication is undisturbed.
Minor word-order variants do not affect τὸν υἱὸν τὸν μονογενῆ ἔδωκεν. The unique-Son predicate and the aorist of giving are stable.

variants.note: ECM not yet published for John, Colossians, Psalms, or Hebrews (none of the anchors fall in the ingested 3 John window). Variant assessments drawn from the NA28 apparatus and INTF NTVMR images, not from CBGM data.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the imperfect ἦν, the πρό and παρά prepositions with creation-frame genitives (John 17:5, 17:24, Col 1:17), the πρωτότοκος that precedes the Son's entry into the world (Heb 1:6), and the sending of an already monogenēs Son (1 John 4:9 perfect, John 3:16 aorist) as marking a pre-temporal Father-Son relation. The begetting texts are read as enthronement declarations of an already existing Son.

Takes the begetting vocabulary at its strongest. yalad (Ps 2:7, Qal perfect) and gennaō (Heb 1:5, 5:5, Acts 13:33, perfect with σήμερον, today) are tied by the canon itself to a moment, and Acts 13:33 anchors the today to the resurrection. On this reading the Son title or its full investiture is constituted or publicly declared at an event in time. This lens grants the pre-existence of the Logos but locates the formal sonship at enthronement, and the begetting words do not lexically rank against it.

Leans on Luke 1:35, where κληθήσεται υἱὸς θεοῦ (will be called Son of God) attaches the title to τὸ γεννώμενον, the one conceived and born. On this reading sonship names the relation the eternal Word enters at the incarnation. It must still account for John 17:24, the Father loving me before the foundation of the world, which addresses the same personal subject prior to creation.

Accepts pre-existence but reads μείζων (John 14:28) and Father-as-source language as marking ontological ranking. Lexically this still yields an asymmetrical relation rather than a temporal beginning for the Son.

Treats Ps 2:7 plus the resurrection σήμερον of Acts 13:33 as constituting sonship at the resurrection. This cannot account for the imperfect ἦν of John 1:1-2, the πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι of John 17:5, or the pre-creation εἰκών and agency predications of Col 1:15-17, which describe a relation already in place before creation.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on two bodies of vocabulary the words do not rank against each other. One body (durative imperfect ἦν, πρό and παρά with creation-frame genitives, the ἐν, διά, εἰς agency triad, πρωτότοκος preceding entry into the world, sending of an already monogenēs Son) describes a pre-creation Father-Son relation. The other body (the begetting verbs yalad and gennaō, attached by the canon to σήμερον and the resurrection, with the future Davidic adoption formula of 2 Sam 7:14) attaches son-installation language to a moment in time. The affirm rests on the first body, the begetting texts are read as declaration rather than origination, and a reader who weights the begetting texts as constitutive reaches a different verdict.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Examine whether the Son is presented in the canon as having a temporal origin or an event that constitutes his sonship, or as eternally and relationally Son of the Father.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem assumes the conciliar vocabulary co-eternal and co-equal, which is post-canonical formulation. The verdict is derived on the original stem, but the neutralized form lets the lexical pattern speak first. Verdict affirms unchanged from the prior file. The lexical evidence still supports affirm via the durative and pre-creation vocabulary, but confidence is lowered from high to medium because the begetting verbs yalad and gennaō carry an origin sense and the canon attaches today, I have begotten you to the resurrection and enthronement (Acts 13:33), and Luke 1:35 ties the called Son of God title to the one being born, so the begetting and title vocabulary underdetermines whether sonship is eternal or constituted at an event. This file is flagged lexically-disputed for that reason.

lay_summary: Two sets of words pull in different directions, which is why this question is genuinely contested at the text level. One set clearly puts the Son before the created order. John 1:1 uses the durative was, the imperfect of the verb to be, three times for the Word at the beginning, while verse 3 switches to came to be for created things, so the Word sits on the uncreated side. John 17:5 and 17:24 have Jesus speak of glory he had and of the Father loving me before the world existed and before its foundation. Colossians 1:15-17 makes the Son the one in whom, through whom, and for whom everything was made, and before all things. Hebrews 1:6 already calls him the firstborn when God brings him into the world. The word only-begotten, monogenes, is used elsewhere of ordinary only-children, so it means unique, not created, and the verbs of sending and giving (1 John 4:9, John 3:16) act on a Son who is already unique. The other set of words attaches sonship to a moment. Psalm 2:7 says today I have begotten you, using a begetting verb whose ordinary sense across hundreds of uses is literal physical birth, and it sits inside a royal decree. Hebrews 1:5, Hebrews 5:5, and Acts 13:33 quote this with today and a perfect have begotten, and Acts ties the today to the resurrection, while Hebrews 1:5 also quotes the royal adoption promise I will be his father, he shall be my son. Luke 1:35 says the child to be born will be called Son of God. The begetting and title words by themselves do not say whether sonship is eternal or begun at an event. The verdict lands on affirm because the durative and before-creation words describe a relation already in place, and the begetting texts read naturally as a declaration or enthronement of an already existing Son. But because the begetting vocabulary genuinely carries an origin sense and the canon applies it to a point in time, the confidence is medium and readers who weight those texts as constitutive reach a different conclusion.
